why: one of the eight the first report could not explain, and it decomposes into two changes that both have a reason. (1) The payload is `(const uint8_t*, size_t)` where rcl takes `void* ros_feedback`: and the payload is CDR bytes (`const uint8_t*, size_t`) rather than rcl's `void* ros_message`, because the C ABI has no runtime typesupport -- the only publish in the whole C surface is `rclc_publish_raw`. See the pubsub stage's `c:publish_raw` and `c:message_type_t`. (2) The goal is a SEPARATE parameter beside the server, where rcl takes the server alone and rclc takes the goal handle alone. rcl can, because its `void* ros_feedback` is the whole `<Action>_FeedbackMessage` envelope and the goal_id is a FIELD inside it; rclc can, because `rclc_action_goal_handle_t` carries a pointer back to its server. Ours can do neither: RFC-0069 makes the core write the envelope (one CDR header, then the goal id, then the fields) so the caller supplies only the inner feedback and the id must arrive as an argument, and our goal handle is a 16-byte UUID TOKEN, not an owning object: `rclc_goal_handle_t` holds the uuid and nothing else, and every lifecycle fact lives in the executor's static goal arena (read back with `rclc_action_get_goal_status`). rcl's `rcl_action_goal_handle_t` is allocator-constructed, carries its own state machine and is finalised by the caller -- no allocator, so there is nothing to construct, nothing to fini, and no object to hang the lifecycle methods on. It is also why our terminal verbs take `(server, goal)` where rclcpp's are members: see `c:action_succeed`. Both halves follow from decisions taken elsewhere, so this is a divergence rather than an unexplained signature -- but it is the widest signature in the action API and it is worth saying that the L1 sibling `nros_action_server_publish_feedback_raw` spells the same call `(server, goal_id[16], feedback_cdr, len)`, i.e. the same four values with a different goal spelling.
